fields.lead: Microbiology is now about communities rather than isolates: uncultured diversity, the microbiome, antibiotic tolerance and microbial immune systems that became genome-editing tools.

papers.title: Phylogenetic structure of the prokaryotic domain: the primary kingdoms
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.why: Used ribosomal RNA sequences to show that life splits into three deep lineages, with archaea separate from bacteria. Every modern tree of life and every metagenomic survey still builds on this ribosomal-gene framework.

papers.title: Quorum sensing in bacteria: the LuxR-LuxI family of cell density-responsive transcriptional regulators
papers.why: Showed that bacteria talk to each other with diffusible signals and coordinate gene expression by population density. Bacterial communication and its disruption remain central to virulence and community research.

papers.title: Microbial biofilms
papers.why: Argued that most bacteria in nature and in infections live as surface-attached communities, not free-floating cells. That reframed chronic infection, antibiotic failure and the physical ecology of microbes.

papers.title: Bacterial persistence as a phenotypic switch
papers.why: Followed single cells to show that a small fraction switch into a dormant, drug-tolerant state without any mutation. This is the basis for today's work on antibiotic tolerance and relapsing infections.

papers.title: Environmental genome shotgun sequencing of the Sargasso Sea
papers.why: Sequenced DNA straight from seawater and found enormous unseen diversity and new genes. It opened the era of metagenomics, in which most microbes are studied without culturing them.

papers.title: An obesity-associated gut microbiome with increased capacity for energy harvest
papers.why: Showed that gut microbial communities differ with host metabolic state and can transfer a trait when transplanted. It launched the causal-microbiome agenda, whose claims and limits are still being tested.

papers.title: Structure, function and diversity of the healthy human microbiome
papers.why: Mapped what a normal human microbiome looks like across body sites and people. Every microbiome-and-disease claim since is measured against this baseline.

papers.title: Complex archaea that bridge the gap between prokaryotes and eukaryotes
papers.why: Found Asgard archaea carrying many genes once thought unique to eukaryotes. It reshaped the debate on how complex cells arose, now framed as a two-domain tree with eukaryotes nested inside archaea.

papers.title: Unusual biology across a group comprising more than 15% of domain Bacteria
papers.why: Revealed the candidate phyla radiation, a huge branch of tiny, uncultured bacteria with stripped-down genomes. It forced a rethink of how much bacterial diversity we had been missing.

papers.title: Isolation of an archaeon at the prokaryote–eukaryote interface
papers.why: After twelve years of culturing, grew an Asgard archaeon in the lab and saw how it might have partnered with bacteria. It turned the origin of complex cells from inference into something you can study directly.

more.title: A molecular view of microbial diversity and the biosphere
more.why: Argued for surveying microbes by their ribosomal RNA genes instead of culturing them. That move is why most of today's microbial diversity is known only from sequence.

more.title: The uncultured microbial majority
more.why: Took stock of the bacterial phyla known only from DNA. The gap it described between what lives out there and what grows in a dish still drives the field.

more.title: Persister cells, dormancy and infectious disease
more.why: Made the case that dormant persister cells, not resistance genes, explain many relapsing infections. Antibiotic tolerance is now a field of its own.

more.title: Transfer of carbohydrate-active enzymes from marine bacteria to Japanese gut microbiota
more.why: Showed gut bacteria in people who eat seaweed picked up seaweed-digesting genes from ocean bacteria. A clean example of diet shaping the microbiome through gene transfer.

more.title: A communal catalogue reveals Earth's multiscale microbial diversity
more.why: The Earth Microbiome Project's standardized survey of tens of thousands of samples across the planet. It set the template for comparing microbial communities at global scale.

more.title: Systematic discovery of antiphage defense systems in the microbial pan-genome
more.why: Found ten new bacterial immune systems by looking at genes clustered near known defences. It opened today's flood of discoveries about how bacteria fight viruses.

more.title: A standardized bacterial taxonomy based on genome phylogeny substantially revises the tree of life
more.why: Rebuilt bacterial classification from genomes rather than from history and physiology. Its GTDB taxonomy is now the default in microbiome research.

more.title: A new genomic blueprint of the human gut microbiota
more.why: Assembled nearly 2,000 previously unknown gut species straight from metagenomes. It showed how much of our own microbiome was still uncharacterised.

more.title: A genomic catalog of Earth's microbiomes
more.why: Recovered over 50,000 genomes from environmental samples worldwide, greatly widening the known tree of life. It is a standard reference for uncultured diversity.

more.title: Global burden of bacterial antimicrobial resistance in 2019: a systematic analysis
more.why: The first comprehensive estimate of deaths tied to drug-resistant bacteria, putting them among the leading causes of death worldwide. It frames current resistance policy.

fields.lead: Virology is working to map the full virosphere through metagenomics, trace how viruses cross species and evolve, and build structure-guided countermeasures for emerging pathogens.

papers.title: Viral RNA-dependent DNA polymerase
papers.why: Reported an enzyme in tumor viruses that copies RNA into DNA, overturning the one-way flow of genetic information. Reverse transcription underlies retrovirology, HIV therapy and a large part of genome biology.

papers.title: Isolation of a T-lymphotropic retrovirus from a patient at risk for acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS)
papers.why: Isolated the virus that causes AIDS from a patient's lymph node. It made HIV diagnosis and drug development possible and remains the model case of a virus-driven chronic disease.

papers.title: The 1.2-megabase genome sequence of Mimivirus
papers.why: Sequenced a virus larger than some bacteria, with genes for translation-related functions. Giant viruses blurred the line between viruses and cells and fed ongoing arguments about viral origins.

papers.title: Bats are natural reservoirs of SARS-like coronaviruses
papers.why: Traced the SARS coronavirus to horseshoe bats. It set the template for finding animal reservoirs of emerging viruses and for judging spillover risk.

papers.title: Host and viral traits predict zoonotic spillover from mammals
papers.why: Built a database of mammal hosts and their viruses and asked which ones end up infecting people. It made spillover risk something you can model rather than only narrate.

papers.title: Origins and evolution of viruses of eukaryotes: the ultimate modularity
papers.why: Laid out viruses as mosaics assembled from reusable gene modules, and proposed evolutionary groupings across all RNA and DNA viruses. It is a core reference for the current effort to classify viruses by deep ancestry.

papers.title: Uncovering Earth's virome
papers.why: Mined huge sequence collections to catalog hundreds of thousands of uncultivated viral genomes across habitats. It showed that most viral diversity is invisible to culture-based virology.

papers.title: Redefining the invertebrate RNA virosphere
papers.why: Sequenced RNA viruses from invertebrates and found many new families, including lineages bridging known groups. It established that RNA virus diversity and evolutionary history were far broader than disease-focused sampling suggested.

papers.title: A pneumonia outbreak associated with a new coronavirus of probable bat origin
papers.why: Identified and sequenced SARS-CoV-2 and showed its close relationship to a bat coronavirus and its use of the ACE2 receptor. It anchors the ongoing work on the origin and spillover of the pandemic virus.

papers.title: Cryo-EM structure of the 2019-nCoV spike in the prefusion conformation
papers.why: Solved the structure of the SARS-CoV-2 spike within weeks of the genome release, enabling stabilized-spike vaccines. It exemplifies the structure-first route to vaccines and antibodies now used for other viruses.

more.title: RNA-dependent DNA polymerase in virions of Rous sarcoma virus
more.why: Published alongside Baltimore, it showed that information can flow from RNA back to DNA. Reverse transcription underlies retrovirology, HIV drugs and much of molecular biology.

more.title: Expression of animal virus genomes
more.why: Sorted viruses by how they get from genome to messenger RNA. The Baltimore classes are still how virologists organise the virosphere.

more.title: Selforganization of matter and the evolution of biological macromolecules
more.why: Introduced the quasispecies idea and the error threshold. Debates about how fast-mutating RNA viruses evolve still start here.

more.title: Viruses in the sea
more.why: Showed that marine viruses are the most abundant biological entities and a major force in ocean nutrient cycles. Viral ecology grew from this picture.

more.title: Structure-based design of a fusion glycoprotein vaccine for respiratory syncytial virus
more.why: Locked the RSV fusion protein in its pre-fusion shape to make a far better vaccine antigen. The same approach later shaped COVID-19 and the first licensed RSV vaccines.

more.title: A highly abundant bacteriophage discovered in the unknown sequences of human faecal metagenomes
more.why: Found crAssphage, the most common virus in the human gut, hidden in unassigned sequence data. It showed how much of the human virome had been invisible.

more.title: Pathways to zoonotic spillover
more.why: Framed spillover as a chain of barriers a virus must pass between animal reservoir and human infection. Much current surveillance thinking follows this frame.

more.title: The evolutionary history of vertebrate RNA viruses
more.why: Sequenced RNA viruses across fish, amphibians, reptiles and more, finding that many virus families are as old as their vertebrate hosts. It reframed virus evolution as long-term co-divergence plus host jumps.

more.authors: Coronaviridae Study Group of the ICTV
more.title: The species Severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus: classifying 2019-nCoV and naming it SARS-CoV-2
more.why: Placed the new virus in the existing SARS-related species and gave it its name. It is the reference point for how SARS-CoV-2 relates to its relatives.

more.title: The Huanan Seafood Wholesale Market in Wuhan was the early epicenter of the COVID-19 pandemic
more.why: Mapped the earliest known COVID-19 cases and found they clustered around the Huanan market. It is central to the still-contested debate over the pandemic's origin.

fields.lead: Immunology is focused on how innate sensing steers adaptive responses, how tolerance and exhaustion are controlled, and how to harness these checkpoints to treat cancer and autoimmunity.

papers.title: Two types of murine helper T cell clone. I. Definition according to profiles of lymphokine activities and secreted proteins
papers.why: Showed that helper T cells fall into distinct subsets with different cytokine programs. The Th1/Th2 idea and its descendants are the basis for how immune responses are classified and tuned.

papers.title: Selective rejection of H-2-deficient lymphoma variants suggests alternative immune defence strategy
papers.why: Found that cells missing MHC class I are killed by natural killer cells, the 'missing self' idea. It framed how inhibitory receptors let immune cells distinguish healthy from stressed or tumor cells.

papers.title: Approaching the asymptote? Evolution and revolution in immunology
papers.venue: Cold Spring Harbor Symposia on Quantitative Biology
papers.why: Argued that adaptive immunity needs innate pattern recognition to switch on, and predicted germline receptors for microbial patterns. This essay redirected the field toward innate immunity.

papers.title: Tolerance, danger, and the extended family
papers.why: Proposed that the immune system responds to signals of tissue damage rather than just foreignness. The danger model still shapes thinking on sterile inflammation, autoimmunity and tumor immunity.

papers.title: Enhancement of antitumor immunity by CTLA-4 blockade
papers.why: Showed that blocking an inhibitory receptor on T cells let mice reject tumors. It launched checkpoint-blockade immunotherapy, now a pillar of cancer treatment.

papers.title: Defective LPS signaling in C3H/HeJ and C57BL/10ScCr mice: mutations in Tlr4 gene
papers.why: Identified Toll-like receptor 4 as the sensor for bacterial lipopolysaccharide by positional cloning. It gave molecular proof for innate pattern recognition and opened the whole field of innate sensing.

papers.title: Involvement of PD-L1 on tumor cells in the escape from host immune system and tumor immunotherapy by PD-L1 blockade
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.why: Showed that tumors exploit PD-L1 to evade T cells and that blocking it restores attack. It led to the PD-1/PD-L1 drugs that dominate current oncology immunotherapy.

papers.title: Control of regulatory T cell development by the transcription factor Foxp3
papers.why: Showed that Foxp3 is the master regulator of regulatory T cells, the cells that restrain immune responses. It anchors current work on tolerance, autoimmunity and Treg-based therapies.

papers.title: T cell exhaustion
papers.why: Synthesized how chronic infection and tumors drive T cells into a dysfunctional but persistent state. This concept explains why checkpoint therapy works in some patients and is central to cell therapy design.

papers.title: Trained immunity: a program of innate immune memory in health and disease
papers.why: Argued that innate cells keep an epigenetic memory of past challenges that changes later responses. It broke the rule that only adaptive immunity has memory and links to vaccines, chronic inflammation and cardiovascular disease.

more.title: Identification of a novel cell type in peripheral lymphoid organs of mice
more.why: Described dendritic cells, the sentinels that show antigens to T cells. Much of today's vaccine and immunotherapy design runs through them.

more.title: Restriction of in vitro T cell-mediated cytotoxicity in lymphocytic choriomeningitis within a syngeneic or semiallogeneic system
more.why: Showed T cells recognise antigen only alongside the body's own MHC molecules. MHC restriction is still the core of how T-cell recognition is understood.

more.title: Somatic generation of antibody diversity
more.why: Explained how a limited genome makes a near-limitless range of antibodies by reshuffling gene segments. It is the basis of how the adaptive immune repertoire is studied and engineered.

more.title: Induced expression of PD-1, a novel member of the immunoglobulin gene superfamily, upon programmed cell death
more.why: Discovered PD-1, which turned out to be a brake on T cells. Blocking it became one of the main pillars of modern cancer treatment.

more.title: Immunologic self-tolerance maintained by activated T cells expressing IL-2 receptor α-chains (CD25)
more.why: Identified the regulatory T cells that stop the immune system attacking the body. Treg biology now drives work on autoimmunity, transplants and cancer.

more.title: A human homologue of the Drosophila Toll protein signals activation of adaptive immunity
more.why: Found the first human Toll-like receptor and showed it switches on adaptive immunity. It confirmed the pattern-recognition idea that innate sensing gates the whole response.

more.title: Immunological mechanisms of vaccination
more.why: Laid out what is known and unknown about why vaccines work, from innate sensing to memory. It frames the systems-vaccinology work that followed.

more.title: Transcriptional control of effector and memory CD8+ T cell differentiation
more.why: Pulled together how killer T cells decide between short-lived effector and long-lived memory fates. That fate choice is central to vaccines and cell therapies.

more.title: Role of the microbiota in immunity and inflammation
more.why: Showed how the microbes we carry tune immune development and inflammation. The microbiome-immunity link is one of the field's busiest frontiers.

more.title: CAR T cell immunotherapy for human cancer
more.why: Reviewed how engineered T cells went from lab idea to approved cancer drug. It sets out the open problems the field is working on now, from solid tumours to toxicity.

fields.lead: Plant biology is now working out how plants sense pathogens and hormones at the molecular level, how they manage their microbiomes, and how to engineer photosynthesis and crops.

papers.title: Analysis of the genome sequence of the flowering plant Arabidopsis thaliana
papers.why: Delivered the first complete flowering-plant genome. It turned Arabidopsis into the reference system whose gene catalogs and mutants still underpin most plant molecular work.

papers.title: FLS2: an LRR receptor-like kinase involved in the perception of the bacterial elicitor flagellin in Arabidopsis
papers.why: Identified the receptor kinase that detects bacterial flagellin at the cell surface. It established surface pattern recognition in plants and the receptor-kinase signaling paradigm.
papers.note: Search budget ran out before this one could be checked; authors, year, title and venue are from memory.

papers.title: The Arabidopsis F-box protein TIR1 is an auxin receptor
papers.why: Showed that auxin is perceived by TIR1, which targets repressor proteins for degradation. This solved a long-standing question and defined how many plant hormones act through regulated protein turnover.

papers.title: FT protein movement contributes to long-distance signaling in floral induction of Arabidopsis
papers.why: Showed that the FT protein travels from leaves to the shoot tip to trigger flowering, identifying florigen. It is the foundation for how plants time flowering with season and is used in crop breeding.

papers.title: Abscisic acid inhibits type 2C protein phosphatases via the PYR/PYL family of START proteins
papers.why: Identified the long-sought abscisic acid receptors that control drought responses. It completed the core hormone pathway and enabled work on engineering stress tolerance.

papers.title: The plant immune system
papers.why: Presented the two-layer model of plant immunity, with surface pattern-triggered and intracellular effector-triggered defense. It remains the organizing framework for plant-pathogen research and disease resistance breeding.

papers.title: Defining the core Arabidopsis thaliana root microbiome
papers.why: Showed that roots assemble a reproducible bacterial community distinct from the soil. It kickstarted modern research on plant microbiomes and their effects on growth and health.

papers.title: Improving photosynthesis and crop productivity by accelerating recovery from photoprotection
papers.why: Showed that speeding relaxation of photoprotection in tobacco raised biomass in field trials. It is the proof of concept that engineering photosynthesis can increase yield.

papers.title: Reconstitution and structure of a plant NLR resistosome conferring immunity
papers.why: Solved the structure of an activated plant NLR immune receptor, showing it assembles into a pentameric ring. This revealed how intracellular plant immune receptors work and is guiding efforts to engineer disease resistance.

papers.title: Insights into land plant evolution garnered from the Marchantia polymorpha genome
papers.why: Sequenced a liverwort whose small, simple genome shows which regulatory systems were present early in land plants. It made Marchantia a model for tracing how plant hormone and developmental pathways evolved.

more.title: MicroRNAs in plants
more.why: Showed plants use microRNAs to control development, much as animals do. Small-RNA regulation is now a pillar of plant gene control.

more.title: Vernalization requires epigenetic silencing of FLC by histone methylation
more.why: Showed that a plant's memory of winter is stored as chromatin marks on a flowering gene. It remains the textbook-live case of epigenetic memory.

more.title: Perception of the bacterial PAMP EF-Tu by the receptor EFR restricts Agrobacterium-mediated transformation
more.why: Added a second bacterial-sensing receptor and showed these receptors shape resistance. Moving such receptors between crops is now an active strategy.

more.title: Can improvement in photosynthesis increase crop yields?
more.why: Argued that photosynthesis, not other traits, is where the remaining yield gains lie. It set the agenda for today's photosynthesis-engineering projects.

more.title: Developmental patterning by mechanical signals in Arabidopsis
more.why: Showed physical stress in growing tissue guides how plant cells orient their growth. Mechanics is now treated as a signal alongside hormones.

more.title: Revealing structure and assembly cues for Arabidopsis root-inhabiting bacterial microbiota
more.why: Published with Lundberg et al., it showed roots recruit a consistent bacterial community from soil. Root microbiome research grew out of these two papers.

more.title: Genomic analyses provide insights into the history of tomato breeding
more.why: Resequenced hundreds of tomatoes to trace domestication and breeding in the genome. It is a model for how crop history is now read from DNA.

more.title: 1,135 genomes reveal the global pattern of polymorphism in Arabidopsis thaliana
more.why: Mapped natural genetic variation across the model plant's global range. It is the reference for studying how plants adapt to their environments.

more.title: Synthetic glycolate metabolism pathways stimulate crop growth and productivity in the field
more.why: Engineered a shortcut around a wasteful step in photosynthesis and got bigger plants in field trials. A key proof that photosynthesis engineering can work outside the lab.

more.title: The ZAR1 resistosome is a calcium-permeable channel triggering plant immune signaling
more.why: Showed the plant resistosome works by opening a calcium channel in the membrane. It explained how immune receptor activation turns into cell death.

fields.lead: Animal behavior is now concerned with collective behavior, animal culture and cognition, consistent individual personalities, and tracking movement at scale with new technology.

papers.title: On aims and methods of ethology
papers.why: Set out four distinct questions about any behavior: causation, development, function and evolution. Researchers still use this framework to organize and separate explanations.

papers.title: Social semantics: altruism, cooperation, mutualism, strong reciprocity and group selection
papers.why: Untangled the competing vocabularies for social behaviour that kept biologists and economists talking past each other. It is the standard map for current debates about cooperation.

papers.title: The evolution of reciprocal altruism
papers.why: Explained how cooperation among unrelated individuals can evolve through repeated exchange. It shaped decades of work on cooperation, cheating detection and social cognition.

papers.title: Ecology, sexual selection, and the evolution of mating systems
papers.why: Tied mating systems to how resources and mates can be monopolized. This ecological logic still structures research on sexual selection and mating strategies.

papers.title: Episodic-like memory during cache recovery by scrub jays
papers.why: Showed that jays remember what they hid, where and how long ago, challenging claims that such memory is uniquely human. It opened rigorous comparative work on animal cognition.
papers.note: Could not confirm via search (search budget exhausted); citation from memory, please check.

papers.title: Cultures in chimpanzees
papers.why: Compared long-term field sites and found many behaviors that vary by community and not by ecology. It established that wild animals have socially transmitted traditions and spurred research on animal culture.
papers.note: Could not confirm via search (search budget exhausted); citation from memory, please check.

papers.title: Culture in whales and dolphins
papers.why: Reviewed evidence for socially learned behavior in cetaceans, including group-specific vocal dialects. It extended animal culture beyond primates and fuels debates about gene-culture coevolution.
papers.note: Could not confirm via search (search budget exhausted); citation from memory, please check.

papers.title: Behavioral syndromes: an ecological and evolutionary overview
papers.why: Argued that individuals differ consistently in boldness, aggression and activity, and that these traits correlate. Animal personality is now a major research area linking behavior to ecology and fitness.
papers.note: Could not confirm via search (search budget exhausted); citation from memory, please check.

papers.title: Effective leadership and decision-making in animal groups on the move
papers.why: Modeled how a small informed minority can steer a whole group without explicit signals. It is a landmark of collective-behavior research connecting simple rules to group decisions.
papers.note: Could not confirm via search (search budget exhausted); citation from memory, please check.

papers.title: A movement ecology paradigm for unifying organismal movement research
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.why: Proposed a unified framework linking an animal's internal state, motion and navigation capacity, and environment. It guides current biologging and GPS-tracking research on migration and space use.
papers.note: Could not confirm via search (search budget exhausted); citation from memory, please check.

more.title: The logic of animal conflict
more.why: Brought game theory into biology to explain why most animal fights are ritualised. The evolutionarily stable strategy is still the field's basic tool.

more.title: Mate selection—a selection for a handicap
more.why: Proposed that costly signals are honest precisely because they are costly. Signalling theory still argues over and builds on this idea.

more.title: Optimal foraging, the marginal value theorem
more.why: Predicted when an animal should leave a food patch for the next one. Its logic now reaches into neuroscience studies of decision-making.

more.title: Female choice selects for extreme tail length in a widowbird
more.why: Cut and glued widowbird tails to show females prefer longer ones. A landmark field experiment that made sexual selection testable.

more.title: The behavioural ecology of personality: consistent individual differences from an adaptive perspective
more.why: Asked why individuals of the same species behave consistently differently. It helped launch animal personality as a mainstream research area.

more.title: Stop signals provide cross inhibition in collective decision-making by honeybee swarms
more.why: Showed bee swarms avoid deadlock with inhibitory signals, much like neurons. Collective decision-making is now studied as a kind of distributed computation.

more.title: Experimentally induced innovations lead to persistent culture via conformity in wild birds
more.why: Seeded new foraging traditions in wild great tits and watched them spread and persist. Strong experimental evidence for animal culture.

more.title: Terrestrial animal tracking as an eye on life and planet
more.why: Reviewed how cheap tags and satellites are transforming the study of animal movement. It maps the data-rich direction the field has taken.

more.title: Shared decision-making drives collective movement in wild baboons
more.why: GPS-collared a whole baboon troop and found movement decisions are shared, not dictated by a leader. It brought high-resolution tracking to primate social behaviour.

more.title: DeepLabCut: markerless pose estimation of user-defined body parts with deep learning
more.why: Made it easy to track animal body parts from ordinary video. Machine-learning pose tracking is now standard in behaviour research.

fields.lead: The field is trying to make biological design predictable, through whole-cell models, engineered circuits, minimal and synthetic genomes and microbial production of useful molecules.

papers.title: From molecular to modular cell biology
papers.why: Argued that cell function should be understood as interacting functional modules rather than single genes. It framed the systems-biology program of studying networks.
papers.note: Could not confirm via search (search budget exhausted); citation from memory, please check.

papers.title: Construction of a genetic toggle switch in Escherichia coli
papers.why: Built a bistable memory circuit from two mutually repressing genes in bacteria. It launched synthetic biology by showing that circuits can be designed from parts.
papers.note: Could not confirm via search (search budget exhausted); citation from memory, please check.

papers.title: A synthetic oscillatory network of transcriptional regulators
papers.why: Built the repressilator, a three-gene circuit giving oscillations in single cells, and revealed noisy behavior. It remains the standard demonstration of designing dynamic behavior.
papers.note: Could not confirm via search (search budget exhausted); citation from memory, please check.

papers.title: Stochastic gene expression in a single cell
papers.why: Measured fluorescent reporters in single cells to separate intrinsic and extrinsic noise in gene expression. It made cell-to-cell variability a central topic.

papers.title: Network motifs: simple building blocks of complex networks
papers.why: Found small wiring patterns recurring far more often than chance in biological networks. This motif idea still guides how regulatory networks are analyzed and designed.

papers.title: Production of the antimalarial drug precursor artemisinic acid in engineered yeast
papers.why: Rebuilt a plant pathway in yeast to make a drug precursor. It is the flagship example of metabolic engineering for industrial production.

papers.title: Creation of a bacterial cell controlled by a chemically synthesized genome
papers.why: Chemically synthesized a bacterial genome and booted a cell with it. It proved genome-scale synthesis is possible and opened genome design.

papers.title: What is flux balance analysis?
papers.why: Explained the constraint-based method for predicting metabolic flux across a whole genome-scale network. It is the standard introduction to modeling cell metabolism, still widely used.

papers.title: A whole-cell computational model predicts phenotype from genotype
papers.why: Built a model integrating all known processes in a Mycoplasma cell to predict behavior from genotype. It remains the reference point for whole-cell modeling ambitions.

papers.title: Design and synthesis of a minimal bacterial genome
papers.why: Designed and built a cell with only 473 genes, and found many of them of unknown function. It shows how far we still are from understanding even the simplest cell.

more.title: Robustness in simple biochemical networks
more.why: Showed bacterial chemotaxis keeps working even when its parts vary, because of how the network is wired. Robustness became a central systems-biology question.

more.title: Engineering stability in gene networks by autoregulation
more.why: Built a self-repressing gene and showed it reduces noise. One of the first tests of a design principle with a synthetic circuit.

more.title: Sniffers, buzzers, toggles and blinkers: dynamics of regulatory and signaling pathways in the cell
more.why: Catalogued the small network shapes that produce switches, pulses and oscillations. A widely used vocabulary for reading cell circuits.

more.title: Foundations for engineering biology
more.why: Argued biology could be engineered with standard parts and abstraction, like electronics. The field's engineering ethos traces to it.

more.title: Network motifs: theory and experimental approaches
more.why: Showed what each recurring circuit pattern does and how experiments confirmed it. It is the field's go-to summary of design principles.

more.title: High-level semi-synthetic production of the potent antimalarial artemisinin
more.why: Took engineered yeast for artemisinin from proof of principle to industrial scale. A case study in what scaling a synthetic pathway really takes.

more.title: Genetic circuit design automation
more.why: Compiled circuit designs written in a programming language into working DNA. It showed genetic design can be automated, not hand-built.

more.title: Programmable protein circuits in living cells
more.why: Built circuits from proteins rather than genes, so they act faster and can go anywhere in the cell. It widened what synthetic circuits can be made of.

more.title: Fundamental behaviors emerge from simulations of a living minimal cell
more.why: Simulated a whole minimal cell through its life cycle in physical detail. It shows how close whole-cell modelling now is to predicting real behaviour.

more.title: Engineered gene circuits
more.why: Took stock of the first wave of synthetic circuits and the modelling behind them. It set out the engineering agenda the field has followed since.

fields.lead: Bioinformatics now centers on large-scale statistical genomics, single-cell data integration, population variant catalogs, and deep-learning models of protein structure and sequence.

papers.title: Basic local alignment search tool
papers.why: Introduced BLAST, a fast heuristic for finding similar sequences. Sequence similarity search still underlies annotation and discovery in nearly all biology.

papers.title: Initial sequencing and analysis of the human genome
papers.why: Reported the first draft of the human genome. It supplied the reference on which nearly all variant, expression and regulation analysis is built.

papers.why: Provided a statistical method for differential expression with few replicates. It is a default tool for RNA-seq analysis.

papers.title: Evolutionary-scale prediction of atomic-level protein structure with a language model
papers.why: Showed that a protein language model trained on sequences alone can predict structure, and applied it to hundreds of millions of metagenomic proteins. It points to the current direction of sequence-based foundation models.

papers.title: Accurate proteome-wide missense variant effect prediction with AlphaMissense
papers.why: Used protein-structure models to score nearly every possible single-letter change in human proteins. It shows where deep learning is taking variant interpretation.

more.title: Identification of common molecular subsequences
more.why: Gave the exact algorithm for finding the best local match between two sequences. Faster methods are still judged against it.

more.title: Profile hidden Markov models
more.why: Explained how probabilistic models of whole protein families find distant relatives. They power protein family databases to this day.

more.title: MUSCLE: multiple sequence alignment with high accuracy and high throughput
more.why: Made fast, accurate alignment of many sequences routine. Multiple alignments feed phylogenetics and structure prediction.

more.title: Ultrafast and memory-efficient alignment of short DNA sequences to the human genome
more.why: Bowtie, released alongside BWA, made mapping millions of short reads cheap. Read mapping is the first step of nearly every sequencing analysis.

more.title: Transcript assembly and quantification by RNA-Seq reveals unannotated transcripts and isoform switching during cell differentiation
more.why: Showed RNA-seq could assemble and count individual transcripts, not just genes. It shaped how isoform-level expression is studied.

more.title: RAxML version 8: a tool for phylogenetic analysis and post-analysis of large phylogenies
more.why: Made maximum-likelihood trees practical for very large datasets. A workhorse for building trees of life.

more.title: Deep generative modeling for single-cell transcriptomics
more.why: Brought deep generative models to single-cell data to handle noise and batch effects. It opened the probabilistic deep-learning approach now common in the field.

more.title: SCANPY: large-scale single-cell gene expression data analysis
more.why: A Python toolkit that scaled single-cell analysis to millions of cells. One of the two standard ecosystems for single-cell work.

more.title: Effective gene expression prediction from sequence by integrating long-range interactions
more.why: Predicted gene expression straight from DNA sequence using long-range context. It marks the turn toward sequence-to-function models of the genome.

more.title: A draft human pangenome reference
more.why: Replaced the single human reference with a set of genomes from diverse people. Moving from one reference to a pangenome is reshaping how variation is analysed.
